title: Starting a Child Care Center in North Carolina: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting a Child Care Center in North Carolina represents a meaningful opportunity to serve working families while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The need for high-quality child care has never been more apparent, and entrepreneurs who can deliver safe, enriching environments are in a prime position to succeed. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (NC DHHS) Division of Child Development and Early Education (DCDEE), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the NC Subsidized Child Care Program, which is supported by the federal Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF).

With a significant market opportunity driven by a massive subsidy waiting list of 12,755 children as of early 2025—a 270% increase in just one year—and reimbursement rates reaching $3,000-$5,500 per month per child, North Carolina offers a high-demand, high-opportunity market for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s star-rated licensing system directly rewards quality, creating a clear path for dedicated providers to build a financially viable and impactful business.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Center in North Carolina, from understanding the critical regulations set by DCDEE to developing your business plan, hiring qualified staff, and preparing for your first inspection. Whether you’re opening a small family child care home or a large commercial center, this comprehensive overview will provide the foundation you need to move forward with confidence.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Carolina’s Child Care Center Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Carolina’s Child Care Center Regulations

Navigating the regulatory landscape is the first and most critical step in opening a child care program in the Tar Heel State. North Carolina regulates Child Care Centers through the NC DHHS Division of Child Development and Early Education (DCDEE), which is responsible for licensing, regulation, and quality oversight for child care centers and family child care providers. The DCDEE’s mission is to ensure that all children have access to safe, healthy, and developmentally appropriate learning environments.

Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks, primarily the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) block grant requirements. These federal rules mandate specific health and safety standards, background checks, and monitoring processes that are integrated into North Carolina’s state-level regulations. Additionally, you must adhere to broader federal laws like the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) to ensure your program is accessible to children with special needs.

The state’s regulatory framework emphasizes child safety, developmental appropriateness, staff qualifications, and quality improvement through its star-rated license system. This system is a cornerstone of North Carolina’s approach, evaluating programs on staff education and program standards. A higher star rating not only signifies a higher quality of care to parents but also unlocks higher reimbursement rates from the state’s subsidy program. Licenses are not permanent and typically require renewal every 1 year, contingent upon a successful annual inspection and ongoing compliance.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Once you understand the regulatory environment, your next decision is to determine the specific type and scale of the child care program you wish to open. North Carolina supports multiple program type variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and physical plant requirements. Your choice will impact your startup costs, revenue potential, and the community you serve.

  • Licensed Child Care Center: This is a commercial, facility-based program that provides care for three or more preschool-age children or five or more school-age children who attend for more than four hours a day. Centers are typically larger and can serve a wider range of ages, but they also have more stringent facility and staffing requirements.
  • Family Child Care Home (FCCH): This is a smaller, home-based program operated out of the provider’s residence. An FCCH offers a more intimate, home-like setting and is often a more accessible entry point for new entrepreneurs. Capacity is limited, but these programs are in high demand, especially in rural areas.
  • Star-Rated Licenses (1-5 Stars): Regardless of the program type, you will be evaluated under North Carolina’s quality rating and improvement system (QRIS). A 1-star license is the minimum standard for compliance. Higher star ratings (up to 5 stars) are awarded based on superior program standards and staff education levels. Achieving a 4- or 5-star rating is a key business goal, as it significantly increases your subsidy reimbursement rates and marketability.

Program size typically ranges from small family child care homes with fewer than 10 children to large centers serving over 100 children. Demand is strongest in rural counties and for specific niches like infant/toddler care, which have the most significant shortages across the state. While urban centers like Charlotte and Raleigh have many providers, rural counties and underserved suburban areas may offer excellent entry opportunities with less direct competition and a clear, unmet community need.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

With a program type selected, the next phase involves establishing your legal business entity and formally beginning the licensing process. A solid legal and administrative foundation is essential for long-term compliance and operational stability.

Providers in North Carolina typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or a Non-Profit organization. Each structure has different implications for liability, taxation, and governance. It is highly recommended to consult with a legal and a financial professional to choose the entity that best suits your business goals.

Before you can apply for your license, you must complete several foundational business steps:

  • Register your business name and entity with the North Carolina Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and filing taxes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (errors and omissions), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Open a dedicated business bank account to keep your finances separate from personal funds.

Once these are in place, you can begin the formal licensing application with the DCDEE. The licensing timeline in North Carolina is a multi-phase process that generally ranges from 4 to 8 months, depending on your readiness and the completeness of your submission. The process includes:

  • Phase 1: Prerequisites (1-3 months): This involves attending a pre-licensing workshop, developing your business plan, and securing a compliant facility.
  • Phase 2: Application Submission (60-90 days for review): You will submit your comprehensive application packet, which includes floor plans, policies, staff qualifications, and more.
  • Phase 3: On-Site Review (30-60 days): A DCDEE consultant will conduct a thorough inspection of your facility to ensure it meets all health, safety, and programmatic standards before a license is issued.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A detailed business plan is your roadmap to success. It is not only a requirement for the licensing process but also a critical tool for securing funding and managing your operations effectively. Your plan should include a thorough financial analysis based on North Carolina’s specific market conditions.

Startup costs for a child care center in North Carolina can vary significantly, typically ranging from $60,000 to $200,000+. This depends heavily on whether you are leasing or buying a property, the extent of renovations needed, your location, and the initial cost of furniture, learning materials, and supplies. Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which represents the largest portion of your budget. In the child care industry, it’s common for staffing to represent 50-60% of total costs.

Your revenue projections should be based on the state’s reimbursement structure. Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in North Carolina include:

  • Reimbursement rates from $3,000 to $5,500 per month per child. These rates are not uniform; the state has over 2,000 distinct rates that vary based on the child’s age (infant care commands the highest rates), the center’s star rating (a 5-star center earns significantly more than a 1-star center), and the county where you operate.

With a strong focus on quality and enrollment, providers operating at a target occupancy of 75% capacity or higher can generally achieve healthy 15-25% profit margins. Your business plan must model different enrollment scenarios and clearly map out the path to reaching break-even, which for many new centers occurs within 12-18 months of opening.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location is at the heart of your child care business. It must be safe, welcoming, and compliant with all DCDEE regulations. Finding the right building is often one of the most time-consuming parts of the startup process.

Facility requirements are detailed and non-negotiable. Key standards include:

  • Minimum Indoor Space: At least 25 square feet of usable indoor space per child.
  • Minimum Outdoor Play Area: At least 75 square feet of fenced, safe outdoor play space per child.
  • Bathroom Facilities: An adequate number of child-sized toilets and sinks must be readily accessible to children.
  • Health and Safety: The facility must have a designated area for isolating sick children, proper sanitation procedures, and secure entry and exit points to prevent unauthorized access.
  • Code Compliance: The building must pass inspections and be in full compliance with all state and local building, fire, and sanitation codes.

When selecting a location, consider more than just the building itself. Your choice should be strategic, taking into account local zoning laws (ensure the property is zoned for child care), accessibility for parents’ daily commutes, proximity to elementary schools and large employers (potential referral sources), and the availability of a qualified workforce in the area.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

High-quality care is delivered by high-quality people. Your staff is your most valuable asset, and North Carolina has specific requirements for qualifications, training, and staff-to-child ratios to ensure safety and quality.

Required roles in a licensed child care center typically include:

  • Center Director: The leader of your program. This individual must have a minimum of a high school diploma, 2 years of relevant experience, and a North Carolina Child Care Director Credential. Their qualifications are a major factor in determining your center’s star rating.
  • Lead Teachers: Responsible for individual classrooms, curriculum planning, and direct communication with parents.
  • Direct Care Staff / Assistant Teachers: Must be at least 18 years old, have a high school diploma or equivalent, and provide daily care and supervision.

All staff, including the director, must undergo comprehensive background checks via the NC Applicant Background Check Management System (ABCMS) before they can have any contact with children. Training requirements are ongoing and include first aid/CPR certification, safe sleep training for infant caregivers, and a set number of annual continuing education hours to maintain and improve skills. These training hours are also essential for maintaining your star rating.

Strict staff-to-child ratios must be maintained at all times:

  • Infants (0-12 months): 1 staff member for every 4 infants (1:4)
  • Toddlers (1-2 years): 1 staff member for every 5 toddlers (1:5)
  • Preschool (2-3 years): 1 staff member for every 8 children (1:8)
  • Preschool (4-5 years): 1 staff member for every 12 children (1:12)

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Written policies and procedures are the operational backbone of your child care center. They ensure consistency, promote safety, and are a key component of your licensing application and subsequent inspections. The DCDEE requires comprehensive written policies covering all aspects of your operation.

At a minimum, North Carolina requires written policies covering:

  • Health and Safety Procedures: Detailed plans for emergencies (fire, tornado, lockdown), first aid, and sanitation.
  • Guidance and Discipline Policies: A clear, positive approach to managing children’s behavior that prohibits corporal punishment.
  • Daily Schedules and Program Activities: A structured plan for daily activities that includes a balance of active play, quiet time, meals, and learning.
  • Staffing and Supervision Plans: Policies that ensure ratios are always met, including during naptime, outdoor play, and transitions.
  • Enrollment, Admission, and Discharge Procedures: Clear criteria for how children are enrolled and when a child may be discharged from the program.
  • Medication Administration Protocols: Strict procedures for storing, administering, and documenting any medication given to a child.

In addition to facility-wide policies, individual care or service plans must be developed for each child, especially those with special health care needs, allergies, or developmental delays. These plans must be created in partnership with parents, reviewed regularly, and documented meticulously per North Carolina and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

With a massive statewide waiting list for subsidized care, your marketing efforts should be less about broad consumer advertising and more about strategic relationship building. Successful providers in North Carolina focus on becoming a trusted partner for agencies that manage child care placements.

Referrals for your child care center will typically come from:

  • County Departments of Social Services (DSS): These agencies are the primary gateway for families seeking subsidized child care. Building a strong relationship with your local DSS office is crucial.
  • Child Care Resource & Referral (CCR&R) Agencies: CCR&Rs are non-profit organizations that help parents find child care. Getting your program listed and highly rated in their database is essential.
  • Local Businesses and Corporate Partnerships: Many large employers are seeking child care solutions for their employees and may offer benefits or direct referrals.
  • Online Directories and Parent-Focused Social Media Groups: Maintaining a professional online presence helps modern parents find and vet your services.
  • Word-of-Mouth from Satisfied Families: The most powerful marketing tool of all. A reputation for high-quality, reliable care will lead to a steady stream of inquiries.

Your most effective marketing strategy is achieving a high star rating. A 4- or 5-star rating makes you a preferred provider for both subsidy agencies and private-pay parents, demonstrating a clear commitment to compliance, quality, and positive child outcomes.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Ongoing oversight is a constant in the child care industry, and staying “survey-ready” is critical for maintaining your license and reputation.

Oversight in North Carolina includes announced and unannounced inspections from The NC Division of Child Development and Early Education (DCDEE). These inspections are comprehensive, with surveyors focused on identifying common deficiencies such as:

  • Improper staff-to-child ratios, especially during staff breaks or transitions.
  • Incomplete staff or child records, including missing background checks, outdated immunizations, or incomplete training logs.
  • Safety hazards in the indoor or outdoor environment, such as unsecured furniture, unsafe climbing structures, or toxic cleaning supplies within reach of children.
  • Failure to follow safe sleep practices for infants, a major point of emphasis for regulators.
  • Inadequate documentation of fire drills, medication administration, or accident reports.

To avoid citations, you must embed a culture of continuous quality improvement and maintain audit-ready documentation at all times. Regularly conduct self-audits, keep meticulous records, and ensure all staff are consistently trained on your policies and procedures. This proactive approach will not only ensure smooth inspections but also contribute to a safer, higher-quality program for the children you serve.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

  • How long does it take to open a Child Care Center in North Carolina?
  • What licenses are required to open a Child Care Center in North Carolina?
  • What reimbursement is available for child care in North Carolina?

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Center in North Carolina is a challenging but immensely rewarding venture. The state’s significant need for quality providers, coupled with a robust subsidy system that rewards excellence, creates a powerful opportunity for entrepreneurs with a passion for early childhood education. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of DCDEE regulations, and unwavering operational discipline.

Providers who invest in creating a safe and enriching environment, hire and train qualified staff, and build strong relationships with referral agencies are positioned for long-term success and community impact. By prioritizing compliance and quality from day one, you can build a sustainable business that makes a real difference in the lives of North Carolina’s children and families.
